newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik hostage drama unchanged as rebel kin arrives.
newsitem.headline: Tajik hostage drama unchanged as rebel kin arrives.

text.p: A Tajik rebel leader returned home from Afghanistan on Monday to help negotiate the release of hostages held by his brother, but appeared to offer little assistance once he arrived, a spokesman for the president said.
The Tajik government had earlier hoped that Rizvon Sadirov could help the week-old deadlock in which his brother Bakhrom is holding 15 captives including U.N. observers and Russian journalists.
But once the two were united in the town of Obigarm, in a mountainous area about 80 km (50 miles) east of the Tajik capital Dushanbe, the president's spokesman became far more pessimistic.
"On his arrival to Obigarm, Rizvon drastically changed his position and supported his brother," Zafar Saidov said.
The first hostages -- four United Nations military observers -- were seized last Tuesday. The rebels later captured a carload of Russian reporters and four workers with the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR.
Two Red Cross workers were captured and then released, but Tajik Security Minister Saidamir Zukharov, who flew in to negotiate with the hostage-takers, was seized early on Saturday.
A senior government source said Ahmad Shah Masood, a north Afghanistan warlord opposed to the Taleban Islamic government in Kabul, was also in Dushanbe to help mediate an end to the hostage crisis.
Masood's forces control the area of northern Afghanistan where Sadirov's fighters are based.
It was not immediately known if he or an aide was actually taking part in any negotiations.

In response to the new efforts at mediation, President Imomali Rakhmonov, whose government faces tough opposition from armed groups of Islamic fighters, called an emergency meeting with his top security officials and a U.N. special envoy, his spokesman said.
Hopes that the captives would be released have been dashed repeatedly and the rebels have ignored appeals from international organisations.
The hostage-taking rebels were demanding free passage for Rizvon Sadirov and his fighters to return to Tajikistan from Afghanistan.
The president's spokesman did not say whether Rizvon Sadirov had been accompanied by any of his Afghanistan-based fighters when he arrived in Dushanbe for the negotiations.
Tajikistan's Islamic opposition fighters operated from bases inside Afghanistan during a four-year civil war with the secular government that was halted by a truce in December.
The Tajik authorities have issued almost daily statements saying the hostages would be released, but two helicopters sent on Friday to collect them returned empty, independent observers said.
